CEO'S ON THE FRONT LINE

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Mines must return to work on April 17th or face permanent damage, Edcon, the largest clothing retailer in the country may not reopen after lockdown. Thousands of jobs are at risk. If the economy was o

Unique Selling Point:
AT LEAST TWO HIGH PROFILE CEO'S ARE PARTICIPATING -WAITING FOR FRONEMAN

Summary:
And if companies in large numbers shut shop, Cyril Ramaphosa’s promises and dreams come to nothing - and political instability could soon become our new normal. Like most countries we are in unchartered territory, but we have a distinct disadvantage – our fiscal cupboard is bare, looted for 10 years by Zuma and his cronies. And then along came Moody’s and as promised downgraded us to junk status. The president’s dithering for two years cost us dearly at our most vulnerable hour. The double whammy left finance Minister Tito Mboweni talk of trembling in his boots. The rand trembled too – down to R18- 65 to the dollar and projected to go to down even further.



Further information:
But as we all tremble in our boots – what can be done? Do we grit it out, or throw our hands up in despair? On the frontlines of the companies that provide jobs, are the CEO’s and the decisions they make with or without government assistance, will be crucial now. So will the role that labour plays. So far it’s been unyielding and threatening, but in the face of mass job losses will they change their tune?

As the country navigates its way through the wreckage of the economy Carte Blanche takes a personal journey with three CEO’s trying to save their companies. Grant Pattison from Edcon who cannot pay suppliers at the end of April and in a teary address to staff on the eve of the lockdown, warned them that Edcon may not open its doors again; Mteto Nyati, the highly respected CEO of Altron who has navigated several companies including IBM and MTN through difficult times, and Neal Froneman, head of the world’s largest platinum group metals miner and one of SA most outspoken business leaders in the country who is not shy to challenge government on where it is taking the economy.

Pattison has already agreed to an interview when lockdown ends, and been asked to do a video diary. Mteto Nyati has also agreed. We are just waiting for Froneman. If not Froneman we can try Mike Teke

Maybe a trip to Rustenburg

CEO’S ON THE FRONTLINE
FINAL SCRIPT TX SUNDAY 26th APRIL 2020 (FACT CHECKED)

Cyril Ramaphosa
Since SA began a nationwide lockdown the pandemic has resulted in the sudden loss of income for businesses and individuals alike deepening poverty and increasing hunger

Our country and the world we live in will never be the same again

DEREK LINK
The Covid19 pandemic is one of the greatest challenges that has ever faced our nation- says Finance Minister Tito Mboweni– the economy is reeling and business leaders are going to have to dig deep- just to ensure their companies survive

Commentary One
On Tuesday the president announced a R500 billion- rand rescue package just to keep companies afloat. But even South Africa’s most iconic brands may still not make it.

At the start of the lockdown CEO of Edcon, Grant Pattison who had just begum to pull the company out of the red, warned Edgars could go into business Rescue, and they would be unable to pay their suppliers

Grant Pattison up sound
In the midst of our own stress and fears we acknowledge the material impact our financial situation has on you and your businesses and the devastating effect our decisions will have on your operations. We can only sympathise with you…excuse me… we hope that we will all emerge from this, and get an opportunity to repair the collective economic damage. Management and the board of Edcon wishes you and your employees and your families safe good health during the upcoming weeks

Commentary Two
Retail, restaurants- no sector is immune as efforts to mitigate against the virus, kills off millions of jobs.

Across the world the airline industry is on the ground, losing billions

Nico
We've never seen in the history of aviation this proportion of passenger aircraft grounded.

Commentary three
Nico Bezuidenhout was appointed CEO of low cost carrier Mango in 2006. A decade later, after a stint as interim CEO of SAA, he left the group. Recently he returned to manage the recovery of Mango, but right now his entire fleet of 14 aircraft are grounded

Nico Bezuidenhout
It takes its toll to see my people scared because we don’t know what is around the next corner, we don’t know how long this is going to last, we don’t know what the full impact is going to be of Covid.

Commentary Four
SAA, Mango’s parent company is in Business Rescue, and this week they called for the liquidation of SAA. Now it’s largely up to Bezuidenhout’s leadership, to save Mango’s 791 jobs, and he has asked his staff to make an enormous sacrifice.

Derek
Now Nico I think you're already asking them to take what a 50 percent pay cut.
Yes
Derek
is the only way the airline can survive.
Nico
It's not the only way but it is some of these measures. And if that means that we have to take salary sacrifices for six months or 12 months then so be it. Mango is our collective baby. It's our collective future and we are committed to it

Commentary Five
He views leadership as a quality that is not just confined to the CEO

Nico
Leadership doesn’t carry a title, leadership doesn’t occupy an office, leadership is in all of us and we need to show that leadership exhibited at every level in the organisation
Derek
Putting it bluntly Nico if SAA goes under does it not necessarily mean that Mango joins in?
Nico
I don’t think it necessarily means that. What assures your existence is having a best practice operation delivering the goods to your guests and to your customers as well as you can

LINK
These CEO’s have all been through the school of hard knocks – and now they are bringing their strategy, their skills and their vision to what may be their toughest business challenge ever

Commentary Six
If there is someone who understands adversity its Altron CEO Mteto Nyati. From his humble beginnings serving customers at his mother’s trading store, he now leads multinational companies and helps them turnaround. In only three years he has doubled the value of Altron.

Mteto Nyati
Thera are always two things that are common in each and every company that I worked for. In terms of strategy one is putting people first, two is making sure the customers and employee agenda is at the centre, and I think it goes back to my upbringing.

Commentary seven
It may be too early to say if the President’s emergency relief this week will avoid a 1929 style depression. Nyati warns there are no quick fixes

Derek
Some say like the great depression do you share those views?
Mteto
The great depression, I think it’s going to be worse, but are we going to be able to come out of it – hey human beings have gone through more difficult situations. We are going to come through this, but my sense is that there is a message coming out of this – that we need to pause and reflect- are we moving in the right direction, are we making the right choices? And as business it’s critical to understand not just focus on shareholders – what about society…. what about our employees- we need to think much broader. This is what this pandemic is forcing us to do.

Commentary eight
President Ramaphosa has promised to forge a new economy in a new global reality, but with an economy that will contract by at least 6%, its going to be tough.

Mining CEO, Neal Froneman believes business is South Africa’s saviour, but he says we are not an investor friendly destination. I spoke to him in America where he is stuck during lockdown

NEAL
What has lacked previously was a lack of clear and decisive leadership we had. We clearly had a split government. We had a lack of alignment and therefore no real decision making. We had a lot of talk but no real action

Commentary nine
In seven years Neil Froneman has built Sibanye Stillwater from a gold company into the biggest platinum producer in the world.

This week 50% of their 80 000 plus miners returned to an entirely different way of working, and Froneman warns- full recovery in mining could take another four to five years

Neal
In fact I go further and say that if you think the challenges around covid19 are big, I think the challenges around growing our economy are even bigger and are going to require much more of what we've seen, than in Covid 19

Commentary Ten
Like all the CEO’s we spoke to, he believes the new bold leadership of Ramaphosa during this crisis could give South Africa the fighting chance it needs

Neal
We need them to make decisions be visible and be firm and act in the national interest not in the party interests.
Commentary eleven
At Altron’s subsidiaries, staff are also adjusting to social distancing. Altron is in a stronger position than many companies, but still, says Nyati 67% of their staff are also concerned about job security

Derek
Millions of people are fearful, and there is a quote that resonates with you: “everything you ever wanted was on the other side of fear
Mteto
Yes and the other quote I like, is that life expands or shrinks in proportion to your courage. Fear will always be there, but the question is how courageous are we to take that next step forward.
Derek
But how do you walk that tightrope Mteto?
Mteto
I think it starts with that vision. If you can see that future yes, I will be able to endure whatever I am going through right now, because I am going for that.

Commentary twelve
As we face that uncertain future, Nyati hopes President Ramaphosa will lead all South Africans through their fears

Mteto
And as leaders we show the way, you will see more and more people being courageous and being able to go to places that they would not go to because they were being led

Commentary Thirteen
Nyati is navigating his company through scenarios, keeping his eye on his long term vision undeterred by Covid 19 and the crisis of the moment.

Mteto
We need to get that thing right. A vision where each and every South African can feel that they are part of this vision. That is very important for me, it’s the foundation of everything.

President Ramaphosa
I have faith in the strength and resilience of ordinary South Africans who have proven time and again throughout our history, that they can rise to any challenge that is presented to our country
We shall recover

We shall overcome

And we shall prosper

THE END




PROMO ONE
Waiters starve, airlines are grounded , and some of our biggest brands are warning of bankruptcy, as CEO’s on the frontlines fight for the survival of their companies.

PROMO TWO
Corporate South Africa is reeling. Will President Ramaphosa rescue package save the day. Three CEO’s on the frontlines share their vision

PROMO THREE
Our country and the world we live in will never be the same again – so says President Ramaphosa. As companies battle to survive- leadership becomes critical
